statement: At one 25,000-capacity festival in England, the first year with an on-site drug checking service (2016, when chemists analysed 247 samples and staff gave results in 230 consultations, with alerts to on-site agencies), compared with the year before (2015): the evidence is insufficient to say whether the service changed drug-related hospital admissions. The festival's figures, from unpublished police reports, were 19 drug-related admissions among 59 admissions in 2015 and 1 among 50 in 2016; admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49 (editors' calculation), paramedics were said to have treated more people on site rather than sending them to hospital, the agencies and indicators behind the records changed between years, and the author states that the pilot cannot show what part the service played. This was testing by chemists at one festival, with one year before and one after and no comparison festival; it says nothing about kits used at home. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: At one English festival, drug-related hospital admissions fell from 19 in 2015 to 1 in 2016, the first year chemists tested drugs on site. But other admissions rose, paramedics were said to have treated more people on site that year, and the way records were kept changed, so the study cannot show that the testing caused the fall. The author says the same.
population: Attendees of one 25,000-capacity outdoor music festival in England, 2015 and 2016
exposure: The festival's first on-site drug checking service (2016): chemists' analysis (FTIR, colour reagents, mass loss) with a brief consultation, alerts to on-site agencies and festival-goers, and a disposal service
comparator: The same festival in 2015, without the service
outcome: Drug-related hospital admissions counted by the festival (from unpublished police post-event reports)
magnitude: Drug-related admissions 19 of 59 in 2015 against 1 of 50 in 2016 (a 95% fall as printed); admissions not classed as drug-related 40 then 49 (editors' calculation). No interval or test. No drug-related deaths at the festival in 2016, a year with six at UK festivals; the author notes that deaths at festivals are rare and often have several causes.

evidence.extracted: Four days at a 25,000-capacity festival in England in July 2016: chemists in an on-site laboratory analysed 247 submitted substances; results were given in 230 consultations with healthcare staff, reaching an estimated 900 festival-goers (an estimate from group size, not a count).

evidence.locator: Meso level impact, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The festival reported 19 drug-related hospital admissions of 59 in total in 2015 (similar to earlier years) and 1 of 50 in 2016, a 95% reduction, from unpublished police reports; festival and partner agencies suggested awareness from alerts, earlier presentation and paramedics' greater confidence in treating drug-related presentations on site rather than sending people to hospital; the author states that the pilot cannot ascertain any contribution of the service, as other variables could not be controlled. Editors' calculation: admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49.

evidence.locator: Pilot limitations and future directions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Partner-agency data varied in quality, with year-on-year changes in the agencies employed and the indicators used, and some data failed to separate drug-related from other incidents or alcohol from drug intoxication; possible unintended consequences, such as displacement to other drugs including alcohol, were not monitored.

Test results were shared with all on-site agencies at daily security advisory group meetings and prompted targeted alerts (chloroquine and ketamine sold as cocaine; high-MDMA pills). There were no drug-related deaths at the festival in 2016, a year with six drug-related deaths at UK festivals, the most on record; the author notes that deaths at festivals are relatively rare and often have several causes.

risk_of_bias.note: One festival, one year before and one after, no comparison festival, unpublished counts whose agencies and indicators changed between years, and more on-site treatment by paramedics in 2016 (ROBINS-I critical).

indirectness.note: Testing by chemists with a consultation at one festival, not kits used at home; hospital admissions only.

imprecision.note: 19 and 1 events in a single before–after comparison, with no interval.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias takes two levels, indirectness and imprecision one each: very low. The fall in drug-related admissions sits beside a rise in other admissions and a change in where paramedics treated people, so it cannot be read as an effect; the author says the same. Status single study.
